items.stem: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, what amount of water forms from 3.0 mol of H₂ with excess O₂?
items.answer: 3.0 mol
items.markingKey: D. H₂ : H₂O = 1 : 1.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the mass of a crucible containing magnesium increases when the magnesium is burned.
items.answer: Magnesium combines with oxygen from the air; the product MgO includes the mass of the oxygen atoms added, so mass increases while total mass (including O₂ used) is conserved.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Magnesium combines with oxygen from the air; the product MgO includes the mass of the oxygen atoms added, so mass increases while total mass (including O₂ used) is conserved. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Iron(III) oxide is reduced: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. What amount of CO is needed to produce 1.0 mol of Fe?
items.answer: 1.5 mol
items.markingKey: C. CO : Fe = 3 : 2.

items.stem: Nia writes: "A balanced equation can be balanced by changing the subscripts in the formulae." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Subscripts define the substance; only coefficients may be changed when balancing.
items.markingKey: Subscripts define the substance; only coefficients may be changed when balancing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
25.00 cm³ (±0.06 cm³) of hydrochloric acid was pipetted into a conical flask and titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide using phenolphthalein. Burette readings are ±0.05 cm³.

Titration | titre / cm³
rough | 22.07
1 | 21.19
2 | 21.21

(a) Calculate the mean titre, explaining which values you used. [2]
(b) Calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid. [2]
(c) Calculate the total percentage uncertainty in the concentration, considering the titre and the pipette only. [2]
(d) State the colour change at the end point. [1]
(e) Suggest why the rough titre is larger than the others. [1]
items.answer: (a) 21.19 cm³ (rough titre excluded) (b) 0.0847 mol dm⁻³ (c) 0.71 % (d) colourless to (pale) pink (e) The titrant was added quickly in large portions, overshooting the end point.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Concordant titres only (rough excluded) (M1); mean = 21.19 cm³ (A1). (b) [2] n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.02119 = 0.00212 mol (M1); c(HCl) = 0.00212/0.02500 = 0.0847 mol dm⁻³ (A1). items.stem: The equation for the complete combustion of decane is balanced using the smallest whole numbers: __C₁₀H₂₂ + __O₂ → __CO₂ + __H₂O. What is the coefficient of O₂?
items.markingKey: B. 2C₁₀H₂₂ + 31O₂ → 20CO₂ + 22H₂O; check O: 62 on the left (+0 in fuel) = 62 on the right.

items.stem: In the thermite reaction used to weld railway lines, 2Al(s) + Fe₂O₃(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(l). A plant needs to produce 1.00 tonnes of Fe per day. (a) Calculate the minimum mass of Al needed per day, in tonnes (1 tonne = 10⁶ g). (b) Calculate the mass of Al₂O₃ formed at the same time. (c) Suggest one reason why more than this mass is used in practice.
items.answer: (a) 0.483 tonnes
items.markingKey: (a) n(Fe) = 1.00 × 10⁶/55.85 = 17900 mol (M1); n(Al) = × 2/2 = 17900 mol (M1); m = 0.483 tonnes (A1). (b) n(Al₂O₃) = 8950 mol; mass = 0.913 tonnes (A1). (c) incomplete reaction/side reactions/impure raw materials/losses (R1).

items.stem: "Stoichiometric calculations based on balanced equations give the mass of product that will actually be obtained." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: They give the theoretical yield; real yields are lower and must be measured.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: give the theoretical maximum quantity; essential for planning industrial processes. Arguments against: side reactions, incomplete reactions and losses in separation reduce the real yield; reversible reactions reach equilibrium. Supported judgement: They give the theoretical yield; real yields are lower and must be measured. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The quantitative relationship between the amounts of reactants and products in a chemical reaction, given by the coefficients of the balanced equation"?
items.answer: stoichiometry
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of stoichiometry.

items.stem: Define the term "state symbols".
items.answer: The symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq) written after formulae to show physical state
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq) written after formulae to show physical state. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which equation is correctly balanced?
items.answer: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃
items.markingKey: C. Atoms: 2 Al, 6 Cl each side.

items.stem: A student claims: "In 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, 2 g of magnesium reacts with 1 g of oxygen." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The coefficients are mole ratios: 2 mol Mg (48.62 g) react with 1 mol O₂ (32.00 g).
items.markingKey: The coefficients are mole ratios: 2 mol Mg (48.62 g) react with 1 mol O₂ (32.00 g). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why is one reactant often used in excess in industry?
items.answer: to ensure the more expensive reactant reacts completely
items.markingKey: to ensure the more expensive reactant reacts completely. Maximises conversion of the costly reactant.

items.stem: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. 1.0 mol CH₄ is burned in 1.0 mol O₂. Which remains at the end?
items.answer: 0.50 mol CH₄
items.markingKey: C. O₂ limiting; it uses 0.50 mol CH₄.

items.stem: Equal masses (100 g each) of TiCl₄ and Mg are mixed for the Kroll process for titanium: TiCl₄(g) + 2Mg(l) → Ti(s) + 2MgCl₂(l). Explain which reactant is limiting.
items.answer: TiCl₄: n/coefficient is 0.527 for TiCl₄ and 2.06 for Mg.
items.markingKey: Converts masses to amounts (0.527 and 4.11 mol) (1); compares with mole ratio 1 : 2 (1); TiCl₄ limiting (1).

items.stem: A student claims: "The reactant with the smaller amount in moles is always limiting." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The coefficients matter: compare n/coefficient for each reactant.
items.markingKey: The coefficients matter: compare n/coefficient for each reactant. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: 18.1 g of Al is mixed with 37.5 g of Fe₂O₃: 2Al(s) + Fe₂O₃(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(l). Determine the limiting reactant and the maximum mass of Al₂O₃ that can form.
items.answer: Fe₂O₃ limiting; 23.9 g
items.markingKey: n(Al) = 0.671 mol, n(Fe₂O₃) = 0.235 mol (M1); compare with 2 : 1 → Fe₂O₃ limiting (A1); n(Al₂O₃) = 0.235 mol, m = 23.9 g (A1).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Using a large excess of one reactant is always good practice."
items.answer: A modest excess of the cheaper reactant is sensible; large excesses are wasteful and are minimised in green chemistry.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ensures complete conversion of the valuable reactant; may shift equilibria to the right. Arguments against: wastes resources and lowers atom economy; excess must be separated and recycled or disposed of, adding cost and environmental impact. Supported judgement: A modest excess of the cheaper reactant is sensible; large excesses are wasteful and are minimised in green chemistry.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A reactant present in more than the amount needed to react with the limiting reactant, so some remains at the end"?
items.answer: excess reactant
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of excess reactant.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the amount of product depends only on the limiting reactant.
items.answer: Once the limiting reactant is used up the reaction stops; the excess reactant has nothing left to react with.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Once the limiting reactant is used up the reaction stops; the excess reactant has nothing left to react with. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

Which change would increase the atom economy of a process?
options: finding a use for the by-product
items.answer: finding a use for the by-product
items.markingKey: C. Counting a useful by-product as desired product raises the effective atom economy; yield and rate do not change the equation.

items.stem: "A reaction with 100 % yield must have 100 % atom economy." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Yield and atom economy are independent: a substitution reaction can give 100 % yield but still produce by-products, so its atom economy is below 100 %.
items.markingKey: Yield and atom economy are independent: a substitution reaction can give 100 % yield but still produce by-products, so its atom economy is below 100 %. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In the combustion of bioethanol, Jonas obtains 6.88 g of H₂O. The theoretical yield is 12.4 g. Calculate the percentage yield.
Calculate the atom economy for making ethyl ethanoate by esterification: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O, where the desired product is CH₃COOC₂H₅.

Ethanol can be manufactured by (route 1) hydration of ethene, C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH, with a single-pass conversion of about 15 % (unreacted ethene is recycled), or (route 2) fermentation of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, with a yield of about 92 %. (a) Calculate the atom economy of each route. (b) Evaluate the two routes, considering atom economy, yield, raw materials and environmental impact.
items.answer: (a) route 1 100 %, route 2 51.1 %; (b) balanced evaluation
items.markingKey: (a) route 1 = 46.08/46.08 × 100 = 100 % (A1); route 2 = 2 × 46.08/180.18 × 100 = 51.1 % (M1 A1). (b) Route 1: 100 % AE, continuous, fast, but uses non-renewable crude-oil ethene, high T/p energy; low single-pass conversion offset by recycling (R1). Route 2: renewable feedstock, low temperature, but AE only 51 % (CO₂ by-product), batch, slow, needs distillation and land for crops (R1); justified conclusion (R1).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "atom economy".
items.answer: The mass of the desired product divided by the total mass of all reactants (or products) in the balanced equation, × 100
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the mass of the desired product divided by the total mass of all reactants (or products) in the balanced equation, × 100. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between atom economy and percentage yield.
items.answer: Percentage yield measures how efficiently a reaction was carried out (actual/theoretical); atom economy measures how much of the reactant mass ends up in the desired product according to the equation.
items.markingKey: Percentage yield measures how efficiently a reaction was carried out (actual/theoretical); atom economy measures how much of the reactant mass ends up in the desired product according to the equation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why chemists in industry aim for a high atom economy.
items.answer: Less waste is produced, fewer raw materials are needed per kg of product, costs and environmental impact are lower – a principle of green chemistry.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Less waste is produced, fewer raw materials are needed per kg of product, costs and environmental impact are lower – a principle of green chemistry. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Atom economy is a better measure of the sustainability of a process than percentage yield." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Atom economy is one useful indicator, but sustainability requires yield, energy, waste, hazards and by-product use to be considered together.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it highlights waste built into the chemistry; encourages addition reactions and catalytic routes. Arguments against: ignores yield, energy use, solvents and toxicity of reagents; by-products may be useful and sold; a full life-cycle analysis is needed. items.stem: "Atom economy is a better measure of the sustainability of a process than percentage yield." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Atom economy is one useful indicator, but sustainability requires yield, energy, waste, hazards and by-product use to be considered together.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "end point"?

The point at which the indicator changes colour, ideally coinciding with the equivalence point
A technique in which an excess of reagent is added to the analyte and the unreacted excess is then titrated to find how much reacted
Titres that agree closely, typically within ±0.10 cm³, used to calculate the mean titre

items.markingKey: B. "end point" is the point at which the indicator changes colour, ideally coinciding with the equivalence point.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "excess reactant"?

In a chemical reaction the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants, as atoms are neither created nor destroyed
A reactant present in more than the amount needed to react with the limiting reactant, so some remains at the end
The reactant that is completely used up first in a reaction and so determines the maximum amount of product
items.answer: A reactant present in more than the amount needed to react with the limiting reactant, so some remains at the end
items.markingKey: C. "excess reactant" is a reactant present in more than the amount needed to react with the limiting reactant, so some remains at the end.

items.stem: Explain the difference between percentage yield and atom economy.
